entries.note: Older in English than espionage, from a Germanic source shared with [[same-root:espy]]; related to [[same-root:inspect]], [[same-root:suspect]] and [[same-root:spectacles]]; first recorded in a 14th-century Bible translation.
Borrowed from French in the 18th century, about 400 years after [[same-root:spy]], from the same source; the word for the overall craft of organised spying.
Given as related to [[same-root:spy]], all of them being about looking.
Given as related to [[same-root:spy]], all of them being about looking.
Given as related to [[same-root:spy]], all of them being about looking.
Related to the source of [[same-root:spy]]; the first recorded spies were basically people who came to look at things, like spectators.
Rarely used now but closely linked to [[same-root:spy]]: a spy is one who espies things.
The French king, successor to the Sun King, who set up the [[see:Secret du Roi]], a network of spies across Europe.
Organisation of [[see:Louis XV]] that sent French spies all over Europe, many of them to Russia.
French spy known as Charles and Charlotte, with masculine and feminine titles, who passed as both man and woman, entering the Russian court; later lived fully as a woman.
Introduced from French during the Napoleonic Wars, where it was used of spies; literally recognition, an etymological doublet of [[same-root:recognizance]].
Checking out an area in advance, common in British broadcasting but unknown to Jess; perhaps said to avoid [[see:reconnoiter]], its pronunciation possibly influenced by [[see:reckon]].
Older doublet of [[same-root:reconnaissance]], originally a formal bond obliging someone to do something; survives in [[see:discharged upon one's own recognizance]].
Released without bail, your signature being the [[see:recognizance]], a promise to come back.
A variant of [[same-root:reconnaissance]] that Jess hates for its pronunciation and Rob would never attempt to say.
A Germanic word meaning to count or consider, unrelated to [[unrelated:reconnaissance]], as discussed in an earlier episode; possibly influences how [[see:recce]] is pronounced.
A knight captured in 1295 who spied for France and became the first Englishman executed for espionage, after royals found letters he wrote about his spying.
A soldier the English sent in 1386 to infiltrate French noble households; executed in Paris, his interrogation exposed a large English spy network in France.
Its sense of secret information gathered by spies, a jargony use of the word for knowledge, dates from the 16th century.
Preventing enemies from obtaining secrets; a 1940s term, much more recent than [[see:intelligence]].
Contains [[from:vestige]] and literally means to follow someone's footprints; despite what Rob assumed, it is unrelated to clothing or [[unrelated:investment]].
Basically putting clothes on, like a vest; from a different root than [[unrelated:investigate]].
From Latin [[from:vestigium]], footprint or trace; first used of where a building once stood, hence something no longer present, as in [[see:vestigial]].
As in vestigial organs, an example of the sense of [[same-root:vestige]] as something no longer active.
Someone who acts, related to [[same-root:act]]; tied to secret agents only from the early 1800s and the [[see:Aaron Burr conspiracy]]; works for an agency without being an employee.
Related to [[same-root:agent]], someone who acts or performs an action.
A plot led by Aaron Burr to create an empire in the American West, during which [[see:agent]] took on its secret-agent sense.
Anyone or anything that provides information to a secret service; like [[see:agent]], an originally neutral term that spy fiction has tied to spycraft.
What spies call their work, an example of deliberately dull, non-specific terms chosen so that anyone overhearing them learns nothing.
A sleeper agent, first found in the 1920s and popularised in the Cold War, chiefly by [[see:John le Carré]]; the OED says espionage took it from spy novels.
Novelist whose books, especially [[see:Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy]], did most to popularise [[see:mole]]; Rob learnt [[see:dead drop]] from them.
[[see:John le Carré]]'s novel, which appears to have done most to popularise [[see:mole]] for a deep-cover agent.
In the CIA glossary, a secret location where material is left for someone else to retrieve; Rob first learnt it from [[see:John le Carré]]'s novels.
CIA glossary term for the tradecraft of secretly opening, reading and resealing envelopes or packages without the recipient knowing.
In use since the 1560s, meaning secret or furtive; based on Latin [[from:clam (Latin)]], secretly, an adverbial form linked to [[from:calare]], to hide.
Latin for secretly, the source of [[gave:clandestine]]; by coincidence the same as the name of the shellfish, but not the source of [[unrelated:clam up]].
Comes from being like the shellfish, not from the Latin word for secretly.
The mollusc is named from an Old English word meaning grip or grasp; the coincidence with the Latin for secretly came up in an earlier clam episode.
Its root means set apart, so the original secrets were things set apart that not everyone could access; compare [[see:secrete]].
Proposed as a [[see:contronym]], meaning both to hide and to emit; secretions are fluids an organ has separated from the body's other fluids.
A word that is its own opposite, discussed in an earlier episode; Rob proposes [[see:secrete]] as one.
Pronounced like cover, as its past participle, until a 1960s American pronunciation influenced by [[see:overt]] took over; from French [[from:couvert]].
From French [[from:ouvert]] and not really related to [[unrelated:covert]], though the two form an elegant rhetorical contrast between open and closed.
Source of [[gave:covert]]; thought to look like [[unrelated:ouvert]] only because a French scholar wrongly assumed the two were related and spelled them alike.
Source of [[gave:overt]], spelled like [[unrelated:couvert]] because a French scholar assumed they were related.
Rob's past tense of spell, perhaps a transatlantic difference; also a type of wheat, which Rob confused with the fish [[see:smelt]].
The fish Rob had in mind when he wrongly called [[see:spelt]] a fish.
An English back-formation from [[from:surveillance]], though also a French word; it means to watch over.
Introduced into English during the Terror, when French surveillance committees monitored people; related to [[same-root:vigilant]] and [[same-root:vigil]] through Latin [[from:vigilare]], to watch.
Related to [[same-root:surveillance]] through Latin [[from:vigilare]], to watch.
Related to [[same-root:surveillance]] through Latin [[from:vigilare]], to watch.
The giant Soviet spy agency, now defunct but still the villain in many spy movies; its work is now split among agencies such as the [[see:FSB]].
An agency that now does much of what the [[see:KGB]] used to do.
Short for Government Communications Headquarters, the UK government's listening service.
The British agency concerned with internal affairs, then as now; numbering such agencies above one makes enemies think there are many more.
The British agency that spies abroad and handles external affairs, the one [[see:James Bond]] works for.
Set up in 1909, just before the First World War; all the British MI sections, such as [[see:MI5]] and [[see:MI6]], came out of it.
The first of the British military intelligence sections, dealing with information about Russia, Siberia and parts of Asia.
The Secretariat, which filed and distributed documents.
Gathered information on particular regions such as the Americas and the Ottoman Empire.
Gathered information on European countries such as France, Belgium, Austria-Hungary and Germany.
Collected and distributed topographical information, including maps drawn from planes flown over enemy trenches.
Responsible for press censorship and military propaganda.
Responsible for cable censorship.
Responsible for postal censorship; as far as is known, the last of the sections.
British designation for 1940s wartime signals intelligence, which decrypted enemy radio and other communications; [[see:Boniface]] was its cover name.
Cover name for [[see:Ultra]]: in Operation Boniface, British intelligence invented an MI6 master spy who ran agents in Germany, to hide its codebreaking.
Meant someone who operates things until the [[see:Pinkerton Detective Agency]] called its agents operatives instead of [[see:detective]]s; broader than [[see:agent]].
Became unpopular for violent strikebreaking in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and started calling its agents [[see:operative]]s.
According to a 1905 New York Press piece, the [[see:Pinkerton Detective Agency]] made the word so offensive that many detective agencies dropped it.
Means hidden, from Greek [[from:kryptē kamara]], a hidden chamber, shortened to Latin [[from:crypta]], a vault or cavern.
Means to hide, relying on the earlier Greek meaning behind [[same-root:crypt]].
The practice of designing or breaking encryption systems, from the same Greek source as [[same-root:crypt]].
A hidden message, solved using spaces and letter frequencies; Jess loves them and wrote literary-quote cryptograms for a 2020 page-a-day calendar.
From Arabic [[from:sifr]], like [[same-root:zero]]; meant any numeral by the 15th century, then a coded message, as French [[see:chiffre]] did first.
From the same Arabic source, [[from:sifr]], as [[same-root:cipher]]; both share the idea of emptiness, as a ciphered message looks like there is nothing there.
Arabic for zero, a loan translation of a Sanskrit word meaning empty, passing through medieval Latin, Spanish, Italian and Old French to give [[gave:cipher]] and [[gave:zero]].
French for any number; it came to mean a coded message because early codes often replaced letters with numbers; the source of [[see:Le Chiffre]]'s name.
Poker-playing villain of the Bond film Casino Royale and its 1960s parody, named from French [[from:chiffre]], number.
Represents letters by the shapes of the grid they sit on; also called the Masonic, Rosicrucian or tic-tac-toe cipher; used since the 1530s and easily broken.
Shifts each letter a fixed number of places; [[see:Julius Caesar]] used it with allies during his campaigns in Gaul, often with a left shift of three.
Used the [[see:Caesar cipher]] when writing to allies in Rome during his military campaigns in Gaul.
Greek device of identical rods; lettered strips wound round a matching rod lined up into the message; how much Spartans and Athenians actually used it is debated.
Louis XIII's cipher by the [[see:Rossignols]], using 587 numbers for French syllables; broken in the 19th century, it may hint at the [[see:man in the iron mask]]'s identity.
A family of French cryptographers who created the [[see:Great Cipher]].
A real prisoner kept in an iron mask for 34 years; the [[see:Great Cipher]] points to [[see:Vivien de Bulonde]], but most historians favour [[see:Ercole Antonio Mattioli]].
French general whom a code group in the [[see:Great Cipher]] suggests was the [[see:man in the iron mask]].
Italian diplomat whom most historians believe was the [[see:man in the iron mask]].
Also the Jefferson wheel cipher: 36 scrambled-alphabet disks on an axle, aligned to spell a message while another row is sent; [[see:Thomas Jefferson]]'s role is uncertain.
Owned a [[see:Jefferson disk]], though whether he invented it or built on earlier devices is unknown.
Puzzle box in The Da Vinci Code, not quite the same as the [[see:Jefferson disk]] but working on a similar mechanic.
Main character of The Da Vinci Code and Angels & Demons, named after [[from:John Langdon]], who designed the books' ambigrams.
Designed The Da Vinci Code's [[see:ambigram]]s and was influential in the modern ambigram; loved imaginative etymology links; died on 1 January 2026.
A design that reads the same upside down, or says something else when rotated 180 degrees; [[see:John Langdon]] helped develop the modern form.
